title: How to Prove Your Team Is Aligned Before a Project Starts
summary: Projects fail when a team assumes it's aligned. Write down where you are and where you're going, and the difference between the two becomes your backlog.
body_markdown:
You've seen this project, where everyone nods along and says "Yeah, we know what we're building." The roadmap looks clean, the timeline feels reasonable, and the vibes are good.


Then someone asks one clarifying question and the whole thing unravels. It turns out nobody agreed on anything, and you'd all been using the same words to mean different things.


By the time you realize the mess, it's too late. Half the budget is gone, management is asking hard questions, your team is demoralized, and the finger-pointing starts.


The way to catch that early is to prove your team is aligned before the work starts.


Projects aren't complicated, since most of the work is follow-through. The hard part is knowing where you are and where you're going, and everything else is just the diff between the two.


## What is AB-Diff?


You define Point A (where you are) and Point B (where you're going) and calculate the difference between them, which is your backlog.


Doing it for real is brutal, and it's supposed to make you anxious.

## Step 1: Define Point A


This is the brutally honest inventory, and there's no room in it for optimism.


Write down what's really there today, even where it doesn't match what should exist or what you thought existed. Who is actually involved and what do they actually own? What decisions have been made versus assumed? What technical debt lives here that everyone pretends doesn't?


The trap is brushing off ambiguities as obvious. When someone says "Oh everyone knows what that means," they don't, and when someone says "you know what I mean," you don't, so stop and make them spell it out.


Every ambiguity is a landmine waiting to blow up your timeline three months from now, so treat each one with anxiety, write it down, and resolve it before moving forward.


Get everyone in a room and force the uncomfortable conversations until you all agree on what the current state actually *is* , before anyone argues about what to do.


## Step 2: Define Point B


Point B is what you're achieving and why.


Focus on the outcome by asking what success looks like in (preferably measurable) concrete terms and why it matters to the business.


Avoid vague destinations like "Make X better" (better how?), "Modernize Y" (to what standard?), or "Build v2" (v2 of what exactly?), because they accumulate scope forever and won't let you move on. A useful Point B is a clear business outcome, like "Migrate A service to B database by C date to achieve D cost reduction" or "Implement A feature by B date to test if it increases user engagement". The most important decisions here are about what you won't do.


The trap here is jumping to HOW before you've nailed WHY. The why is your job, and your team figures out the how. The why tells you whether Point B is even worth reaching, and it guides every decision downstream.


Apply the same anxiety you gave Point A. If for any reason you can't explain Point B to a junior, what you have is wishful thinking and a migraine scheduled a few months from now.


## Step 3: Calculate the Diff


Now work backwards from B to A and list everything that has to change to get there, and treat that list as your backlog.


This diff should be exhaustive, with nothing left implied or assumed, and it should contain everything the layer below you needs to complete these tasks without coming back to ask what you meant.


Break it into pieces your team can execute, with a clear owner for every item and outcomes you can test, so you know when each piece is done. Your job as a leader is to think through the hard, ambiguous, cross-cutting concerns so your team doesn't have to, and to give them clear, bounded work.


Since you've already done the strategic thinking, their job is execution.


## Step 4: Track and Validate


Project tracking becomes almost trivial now. You have subtasks that are either done or not, and that leaves no room for status theater.


The validation test is whether completing every item on this list gets you from Point A to Point B, and if it doesn't, one of three things went wrong.


Either you defined Point A incorrectly, you defined Point B incorrectly, or your diff wasn't thorough enough.


When new information arrives (oh, and it will), update the model and re-diff. That's the process working as intended, since you're catching problems while you can still adapt and before management gets upset.


Take the moment to ask yourself and your team why those items were missed. Were they legitimate blind spots only shipping could find? Were they bad assumptions you held? What do you need to put in place so your next AB-Diff is even better?


## Why This Works


This forces alignment before a single line of code is written, so nobody ends up saying "I thought we agreed" three months in.


This also surfaces hidden work early. All those systems nobody remembered, integrations everyone assumed would just work, and ownership gaps between teams show up in the diff before any of them can cause a production incident.


Naturally, this makes ownership explicit too. Every item has a name next to it, and you stop hearing "I thought you were handling that."


Management couldn't ask for clearer visibility. They can see the backlog and the progress on it, and nobody has to sit through weekly status meetings where everyone performs confidence.


Scope creep is now super obvious. When someone asks for something new, your answer is "That's not in the diff. Want to re-scope Point B?"


## Story Time


A client hired Byte Bot for a legacy migration. They were confident they knew what to do, and they even had a timeline.


Despite some hesitation, we made them define Point A and Point B. Just that exercise, before any planning, revealed a ton of work nobody had considered. They had even forgotten an entire system existed, and there were deployments they'd assumed would "just work."


Then we calculated the diff. Their original estimates would have been wildly off, and we're talking months.


We caught this super early, months before management would have started asking hard questions. The client adapted their timeline, adjusted their budget, and set realistic expectations with stakeholders.


The project still had challenges, but they were ones we'd seen coming and chosen to take on. The team stayed sane, management had visibility without micromanaging, and when the board asked about progress, there was a clear answer with numbers.


Needless to say, they found it valuable enough to extend the contract with us.


## Closing


Forcing clarity upfront shrinks the uncertainty in a project dramatically, and re-diffing is how you deal with whatever is left as new information arrives.
